newsitem.title: HUNGARY: HORN CALLS FOR SOCIALIST UNITY AHEAD OF ELECTIONS.
newsitem.headline: HORN CALLS FOR SOCIALIST UNITY AHEAD OF ELECTIONS.

text.p: The success of Hungary's economic stabilisation is likely to help the Socialist Party (MSZP) repeat its 1994 election victory in 1998, Prime Minister Gyula Horn told a party congress.

Horn, president of senior government party MSZP, said in his opening speech of the two-day congress on Friday that an austerity programme launched in 1995 led the economy to sustainable growth the first time in almost thirty years.
"The rate of (economic growth) will reach the average of the European Union already in 1997," he said.

The 1995 programme, while it had cut the soaring budget and current account deficits, also led to a 17 percent fall in real wages, knocking the Socialists to third place in opinion polls behind two opposition parties.

Horn cracked down hard in his speech on both his leftist critics within the party and right-wing opposition parties which denounce the Socialist-Liberal rule for opening a wide schism between the rich and the poor.

"Hard as it may be, we have to make people realise that the road chosen after 1989 -- the first stage of market economy -- is not determined by morality, but by the accumulation of capital," Horn said.
An alleged corruption scandal at the state privatisation agency APV last year also dealt a hard blow on the popularity of the Socialists and the junior government party Free Democrats.
Horn said his party remained clear of allegations of corruption and the government's merits in improving living standards and reducing inflation would weigh heavy in the balance.
"I am convinced that MSZP has every chance to win the next elections," he said.
The fact that Hungary is likely to begin talks on joining the NATO in September and on European Union (EU) membership in January 1998, is also a credit to the government, Horn said.
He added that Hungary had clear-cut advantages over other countries in the region in productivity, accumulated foreign capital and the reform of the government budget.
"(Other countries) are just beginning to face the problems with which we have been fighting for years."
However, referring to economic difficulties in some economies of the region, Horn stressed that Hungary was not interested in the failure of any of them.

Horn called for unity within the party ahead of the elections, saying that the first and most difficult stage of transition into market economy was over but MSZP had yet to convince Hungarians that future welfare demanded further efforts.

"The society must be prepared that its future will be much easier but the fight is far from over," he said, adding however, that the government did not plan any measures to speed up economic growth artificially.
Hungary expects the gross domestic product to rise at an increasing pace of two to five percent on the next five years.
The next general elections are likely to be held in May 1998.
